title: SQL reference
summary: The SQL from the course, each command with what it does. Copy a card into the query box.

items.label: SELECT everything
items.hint: Shows every column and every row of a table. The star means all columns.

items.label: SELECT some columns
items.hint: Shows only the columns you name, in the order you name them, separated by commas.

items.label: WHERE
items.hint: Keeps only the rows where the test is true. Use =, <, >, <=, >= and != to compare.
items.example: SELECT title, year FROM songs WHERE year > 2015;

items.label: AND, OR
items.hint: AND needs both tests to be true. OR needs at least one. Text goes in single quotes.
items.example: SELECT title FROM songs WHERE genre = 'pop' AND year > 2015;

items.label: LIKE
items.hint: Matches text by pattern. % stands for any run of letters, so %love% finds a title with love anywhere in it.
items.example: SELECT title FROM songs WHERE title LIKE '%love%';

items.label: ORDER BY
items.hint: Sorts the rows. ASC goes low to high (the default); DESC goes high to low.
items.example: SELECT title, plays FROM songs ORDER BY plays DESC;

items.label: LIMIT
items.code: SELECT * FROM ‹songs› ORDER BY ‹plays› DESC LIMIT ‹3›;
items.hint: Stops after that many rows. With ORDER BY it gives a top three or bottom three.
items.example: SELECT title, plays FROM songs ORDER BY plays DESC LIMIT 3;

items.label: COUNT
items.hint: Counts the rows. Add a WHERE to count only the rows that pass the test.
items.example: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM songs WHERE genre = 'rock';

items.label: SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX
items.hint: One answer from a whole column: SUM adds, AVG averages, MIN and MAX find the smallest and largest.
items.example: SELECT MIN(seconds), MAX(seconds), AVG(seconds) FROM songs;

items.label: AS (a nicer column name)
items.hint: Gives a result column a name of your choice, so the table reads clearly.
items.example: SELECT COUNT(*) AS how_many FROM songs;

items.label: GROUP BY
items.hint: Makes one row per group and works out the count, sum or average for each group.
items.example: SELECT genre, COUNT(*) AS songs FROM songs GROUP BY genre;

items.label: JOIN
items.hint: Puts two tables side by side, matching rows where the ON test is true. Name the table before the column: songs.title.

items.label: INSERT
items.hint: Adds one new row. List the columns, then the values in the same order.

items.label: UPDATE
items.hint: Changes values in existing rows. Always add a WHERE, or every row changes.

items.label: DELETE
items.hint: Removes rows. Always add a WHERE, or every row goes.

items.label: CREATE TABLE
items.hint: Makes a new, empty table. Each column has a name and a type: INTEGER, REAL (decimals) or TEXT.

items.label: PRIMARY KEY
items.hint: A column whose value is different in every row, so each row can be told apart and found again. It is the column other tables point to.

items.label: Link to another table
items.hint: A column that holds another table's key (a foreign key). It is how a review points to the song it is about.

items.label: Connect and ask
items.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect('‹music.db›')
rows = db.execute('SELECT * FROM ‹songs›').fetchall()
items.hint: Opens the database file, runs a query and gets the rows back as a list you can loop over.

items.label: A ? for each value
items.hint: Put a ? where a value goes and give the values in brackets after. Never join text into the query yourself.

items.label: Save the changes
items.hint: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE only stick once you commit. Without it the change is lost when the program ends.
